1. PREMISE: Your framing assumes that friendship and romantic detachment can be sustained simultaneously through good intention and mutual affection. The hidden assumption is that the emotional infrastructure binding you—proximity, priority, physical comfort, confessional intimacy—can remain intact while the commitment structure changes. The entire analysis turns on recognizing that sustained contact during the reorganization period will prevent the neurological and behavioral rewiring necessary for either party to form new attachments or to access the friendship genuinely rather than as a substitution for what was lost.

2. STAKES: You face the loss of daily access to someone whose presence shaped your sense of safety and priority; you risk years of partial attachment that forecloses new partnerships. Your former partner faces identical consequences. Any prospective intimate partners of either of you stand to encounter relationships compromised by unresolved asymmetries and divided attention. Your mutual friend group faces pressure to manage allegiances and will absorb emotional labor as you both use friendship as a container for unprocessed grief. The relationship itself—the actual friendship that might exist after genuine separation—stands to be replaced permanently by a ghost-relationship that satisfies neither the need for romantic partnership nor the clarity required for authentic friendship.

3. DIRECTIVE: Establish a period of no contact lasting a minimum of six months before any contact occurs, with no exceptions for birthdays, chance encounters, or moments of vulnerability. The interval allows both nervous systems to recalibrate to the absence and permits new relational patterns to form without the constant pull of the previous architecture.
[Rejected path: maintaining contact while "working through" the transition. This preserves the exact emotional conditions that prevent adaptation; probability of primary harm: high.]

4. RECOMMENDATION: Cease all regular communication and in-person contact immediately and maintain this separation until the acute phase of grief has passed into memory rather than active longing. Sustained proximity during transition directly prevents the formation of new attachments because the original relationship continues to occupy the role of primary emotional witness—every new person becomes a supplement to the existing bond rather than a replacement for it. The competing claim that friendship proves your love has force only if you define love as present comfort rather than as genuine regard for the other person's capacity to build a full life; that definition is outweighed by the concrete harm of indefinite partial-attachment. Therefore: impose a complete cessation of contact now, with the explicit agreement that friendship may become possible only after sufficient time has restored your separate identities.
